questions.question: A child is brought to the emergency department with a large lesion on his forearm. As a surgery resident, you decide to excise the lesion in the emergency operation theatre. Which of the following investigations will test the entire coagulation pathway?

explanation.text: Thromboelastography (TEG) is a coagulation test that evaluates the entire coagulation pathway, including both the intrinsic and extrinsic pathways and fibrinolysis. It offers a comprehensive assessment of clot formation, clot strength, and clot breakdown. Thromboelastography (TEG) is a diagnostic tool used to evaluate coagulation profiles and guide management with transfusions and hemostatic therapies.

Studies show that TEG can reduce blood product usage by up to 40%, decrease postoperative length of stay, and lower the risk of reoperation. TEG measures the viscoelastic properties of blood as clotting occurs. The resulting data is plotted on a graph with time on the x-axis and amplitude (clot strength) on the y-axis. Key values include: Reaction time (R): The time it takes for the clot strength to reach an amplitude of 2 mm.

Kinetics (K): The time from R to when the amplitude reaches 20 mm. α-angle: The angle formed by a line from R to the point where K intersects with the 20 mm amplitude mark. Maximum amplitude (MA): The highest amplitude reached. Lysis at 30 minutes (Ly30): The per cent decrease in amplitude 30 minutes after MA (or 60 minutes in some cases). Inference: A prolonged R time may indicate coagulation factor deficiency or anticoagulation.

A decreased α-angle can result from hypofibrinogenemia Low MA can be due to thrombocytopenia or platelet dysfunction. Increased Ly30 indicates hyperfibrinolysis, often seen in severe trauma or with thrombolytic therapy. Based on the TEG findings, targeted blood products can be administered to normalize coagulation.

For example: Fresh frozen plasma for prolonged R time Cryoprecipitate for decreased α-angle Platelets for decreased MA Tranexamic acid or aminocaproic acid for increased Ly30 Incorrect Options: Activated Partial Thromboplastin Time (aPTT) (Option A) primarily evaluates the intrinsic pathway of the coagulation cascade.
**Prothrombin Time (PT) (Option B):** mainly assesses the extrinsic pathway of the coagulation cascade.
**Bleeding Time (Option D):** measures the duration for bleeding to cease following a standardized skin incision. It primarily evaluates platelet function and primary hemostasis.

questions.question: Which of the following is the most common inherited bleeding disorder?

explanation.text: Von Willebrand Disease (VWD) is the most common inherited bleeding disorder. Types: vWD type 1 vWD Type 2 vWD Type 3 Autosomal dominant. The most common type. Mild to moderate vWF deficiency. Quantitative defect. point substitutions prevent the vWF protein from maturing or cause it to leave the plasma quickly Autosomal dominant. Qualitative defect.

Types: 2A, 2B, 2M, 2N 2A (Most common) - Decrease in binding between vWF and Gp1b/9 missense mutations cause faulty multimer formation → the most active forms of vWF, i.e. large- and intermediate-sized multimers are absent. 2B - Increase in binding between vWF and Gp1b/9 2M - VWF dependant platelet adhesion is decreased. There is impairment of VWF binding to platelets.

Type 2M VWD typically has mild to moderate mucocutaneous bleeding 2N - There is marked decline in the binding affinity for factor VIII. The level of factor VIII is lower when compared to the VWF:Ag. This led to misdiagnosis as haemophilia A Autosomal recessive.

Quantitative defect. produced by frameshift mutations or deletions affecting both alleles (autosomal recessive), which produce little or no vWF. Factor VIII levels are also lowered because vWF stabilizes factor VIII in the blood, and the resulting bleeding condition is severe.

**Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation (DIC) (Option B):** is an acquired (not inherited), secondary condition due to systemic activation of the clotting cascade (e.g., in sepsis, trauma, malignancy).

**Factor V Deficiency (Option C):** is a rare inherited bleeding disorder, also known as parahemophilia. Far less common than vWD. Hemophilia (A or B) (Option D) is an inherited X-linked recessive disorder involving Factor VIII (A) or Factor IX (B) deficiency. More common in males but still less prevalent than von Willebrand disease.
